translation_updates.summary: "On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies" was the third of the four papers Albert Einstein published in Annalen der Physik during his 1905 "miracle year," submitted on 30 June and appearing in print on 26 September. In it Einstein reworked the mechanics of bodies moving at speeds approaching that of light so as to reconcile them with Maxwell's equations for electricity and magnetism. The paper's two postulates, that physical laws hold in every inertial frame and that the speed of light is constant for all observers, became the basis of what was subsequently named the special theory of relativity. Mass-energy equivalence was not part of this paper; Einstein derived that result separately in a fourth 1905 paper published later that autumn.

Franz Brentano, described in this source as an Austrian philosopher, published Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkte in 1874, arguing that psychology should aim to establish exact laws in the manner of the natural sciences. He originally planned the work in six books but completed only two before falling ill, leaving the project unfinished. In it Brentano reintroduced the concept of intentionality into the philosophy of mind, describing it as the mark distinguishing mental phenomena from physical phenomena. The book established Brentano's reputation, helped constitute psychology as a scientific discipline, and influenced Husserlian phenomenology, currents of analytic philosophy, gestalt psychology, and Alexius Meinong's theory of objects.

Principia Mathematica, often abbreviated PM, is a three-volume work on the foundations of mathematics written by Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell and published by Cambridge University Press in 1910, 1912 and 1913. Its central technical device was the theory of types, adopted to rule out the unrestricted comprehension of classes and properties that gives rise to paradoxes such as the Russell set; the ramified version of this theory was specifically Russell's. Although the work's coverage stopped short of real analysis, by its third volume it was evident that a large body of known mathematics could in principle be developed within the formal system PM established. The book went on to popularize symbolic logic and is credited with advancing the subject.

Herbert A. Simon's Administrative Behavior: a Study of Decision-Making Processes in Administrative Organization was published by Macmillan in New York in 1947, its first edition growing out of Simon's doctoral thesis in political science at the University of Chicago. The book treated decision-making as the core of administration and proposed that real administrators are not perfectly rational optimizers but instead "satisfice," settling for a course of action that is merely satisfactory rather than optimal. Simon later wrote that he had built the book squarely on Chester Barnard's The Functions of the Executive and remained deeply indebted to it, while counting the bounded rationality notions among the genuinely novel contributions the book made. Administrative Behavior became foundational to the Carnegie School of organizational economics, and its ideas were later cited in Simon's 1978 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

★ The generator caught a citation-provenance problem in its own draft that QC would have had to work to find. In the Brentano summary, the phrase describing intentionality as the mark distinguishing mental from physical phenomena traces to Roger Scruton-s paraphrase as reported in the article — not to Brentano-s own words — and the article itself notes Scruton finds Brentano-s own passage "obscure and hesitant". The generator flagged this rather than letting a commentator-s gloss read as the author-s. Kept as written because the substance is independently established: SEP-s Intentionality entry, read during Track B QC of this same session, states that Brentano held intentionality to be the hallmark of the mental. Provenance recorded here so a later reader does not have to rediscover it.

It also honoured the nationality ruling exactly — the cited article calls Brentano Austrian while the person node-s sources call him German, and the summary says "described in this source as an Austrian philosopher", carrying the attribution rather than silently choosing. That is the right shape for a source-side discrepancy.

The Einstein paper summary does what the ruling asked and then some: it excludes mass-energy equivalence and adds an explicit sentence assigning that result to the fourth 1905 paper, so a reader cannot mis-attribute it. The Principia summary names Whitehead as full co-author throughout, which matters because the corpus has no Whitehead node — the graph gap is recorded on the edge, and the prose does not paper over it.
